title: When mixing lowers similarity-sensitive entropy: Exact concavity criteria and sharp bounds on entropy gain
description:
Unrefereed research candidate. Exact concavity criteria and sharp bounds on entropy gain.

Context. Ecologists, forecasters and machine-learning researchers often measure the diversity or uncertainty of a distribution with a measure that knows some outcomes are alike: two closely related species count as less diverse than two unrelated ones. The standard such measure, the order-one similarity-sensitive entropy of Leinster and Cobbold, HK(p) = −∑ pi log (Kp)i, averages minus the log of each outcome's typicality, its expected similarity to a random draw. Users expect it to behave like Shannon entropy: pooling two communities should not lower diversity, and an observation should not raise expected uncertainty. Both properties are concavity. Gallego Posada, Vani, Schwarzer and Lacoste-Julien (GAIT) conjectured concavity for positive definite similarity matrices satisfying the multiplicative triangle inequality; Bavaud gave failures without that inequality and asked for exact conditions; Miller found an 18-state counterexample satisfying both conditions and asked for the least number of states at which concavity can fail. A claim that higher orders of the Ricotta–Szeidl family are concave was later acknowledged by Ricotta, Szeidl and Pavoine to rest on a faulty proof.

Main results. (1) A finite test: after identical rows are merged, HK is concave if and only if the reduced matrix is positive definite and one explicit vertex matrix per state is positive semidefinite (Theorem 1); a sign condition on the inverse covers every ultrametric similarity (Corollary 2). (2) The exact minimum: for positive definite similarities satisfying the multiplicative triangle inequality, four states never permit failure (exact polynomial certificate) and a five-state example on the complete bipartite graph K2,3 fails, answering Miller's question. (3) Weighted trees: a linear-time test; a star with equal edges needs at least 13 states to fail. (4) The size of a failure: if K is positive semidefinite or satisfies the multiplicative triangle inequality, an observation can raise expected entropy by at most half the expected posterior entropy, hence by at most (1/2) log n; over positive semidefinite similarities the sharp worst case is (1/2) log n − log log n + log 2 − 1 + o(1). Bavaud's effective entropy lies between one half and all of HK. (5) Joint entropy under a tensor-product similarity is subadditive for every joint law only in degenerate cases, answering the second part of Bavaud's question. (6) Among average-rarity indices only affine profiles are concave for every positive definite metric similarity, so in the Ricotta–Szeidl family only Rao's quadratic entropy is safe. (7) On standard Borel spaces concavity is decided by finite restrictions.

Method. Changing variables from changes in probabilities to relative changes in typicality makes the curvature matrix depend linearly on the distribution, so it suffices to check the corners of the simplex. The four-state case writes every four-point distance as a sum of cuts and checks seven polynomials whose coefficients are all positive.

Limits. Failures are rare and usually small: the five-state example fails throughout a window of edge similarities of width about 0.033 just below the positive definiteness threshold, by about 0.0003 nats at a = 12/17, and the exact test finds no failure on a grid below that window; none of 2000 seeded random five-state examples failed (a numerical observation, not a certificate). The worst case nevertheless grows with the number of states. The four-state step rests on an exact computer certificate, not a conceptual proof. Several equivalences (concavity, nonnegative expected information gain, proper scoring) were already noted by Miller and by GAIT and are credited. The asymptotic statements converge slowly.

Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF) and its figure; classify.py (the exact rational concavity test for any similarity matrix); verify.py (Table 1: the four-state polynomial certificate and the five-state curvature); verify_independent.py (a second, SymPy-based four-state certificate); verify_mixing.py (the five-state Jensen gap and a one-bit tree example); check_classifier.py (classifier checks against the star thresholds and the order-three counterexample); check_extensions.py (cut decomposition, the K2,3 family interval, the star threshold, ultrametric sign checks, the seeded random experiment and the asymptotic table); figure.py; recorded outputs; the bibliography; a machine-readable index; a research-gate record; a review summary; a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Certificate arithmetic is exact (rational or symbolic); every check exits with status 1 on failure, also under python -O. The asymptotic table uses mpmath at 50 digits with a declared comparison tolerance of 1e-9.

Assurance. Written proofs with exact computational certificates. Internal AI-assisted review only: five Claude reviewer roles run as two subagents, the lead's proof audit and clean replay with negative controls, one revision round with extensions, then a re-review and proof audit of the changed material. No second-model (Astra/Codex) review took place. This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.
